title: Weather expressions
subtitle: il fait / il y a / il pleut — pick the right form.
blurb: Pretest yourself on weather grammar before the speed-drill.

items.contextLabel: [Checking forecast] A sunny morning in Paris
items.why: il fait beau — French uses the verb faire impersonally for weather, not être. Il est beau means 'he is handsome' (about a person). The dummy subject il has no real referent. il a and il y a both exist but take a noun phrase, not an adjective (il y a du soleil, not il y a beau).

items.contextLabel: [Checking forecast] Checking the forecast before packing
items.sentenceBefore: En juillet à Paris, il fait très
items.fullSentence: En juillet à Paris, il fait très chaud.
items.sentenceTrans: In July in Paris, it is very hot.
items.why: il fait chaud — 'it is hot'. The adjective after il fait never changes form (no gender/number agreement) because il is impersonal — there is no noun it describes. froid = cold, beau = nice, mauvais = bad (weather). All four follow il fait the same way.

items.sentenceAfter: ce matin — il y a du verglas dehors !
items.fullSentence: Il fait froid ce matin — il y a du verglas dehors !
items.sentenceTrans: It's cold this morning — there's ice on the ground outside!
items.why: il fait froid — 'it is cold'. The clue il y a du verglas (there is ice on the ground) points to genuinely freezing temperatures, making froid the only right choice. frais means pleasantly cool (autumn/spring — you might want a light jacket, but no ice). Know all four: chaud (hot), froid (cold), frais (cool), doux (mild).

items.contextLabel: [Checking forecast] Looking out the window — it's grim
items.fullSentence: Il fait mauvais — je reste à la maison.
items.sentenceTrans: The weather is bad — I'm staying home.
items.why: il fait mauvais — the adjective used after il fait stays masculine singular (no agreement). mauvaise would be the feminine form — correct for a noun like une mauvaise journée, but NOT after the impersonal il fait. mal is an adverb (badly), not an adjective. pas beau is colloquial but not standard written French.

items.fullSentence: Il fait frais mais c'est agréable.
items.why: il fait frais — note the spelling: frais, not fraîs (no circumflex on the i). frais implies pleasantly cool — the kind of weather where you don't need a coat but you wouldn't say it's cold. froid is genuinely cold and would not prompt the comment 'c'est agréable'.

items.contextLabel: [Checking forecast] Deciding whether to bring an umbrella
items.fullSentence: Il y a du vent dehors.
items.why: il y a du vent — vent is masculine, so the partitive is du (= de + le). For feminine weather nouns use de la (e.g. de la neige if you say it this way). For vowel-initial nouns use de l' (e.g. de l'orage). The definite article le vent would mean 'the wind' in general, not 'some wind'.

items.fullSentence: Il y a du soleil et il fait chaud.
items.why: il y a du soleil — soleil is masculine, so du. Note that il fait soleil is NOT standard French (unlike il fait beau / chaud). The correct way to say 'it's sunny' is il y a du soleil or il fait beau. le soleil = 'the sun' (definite); un soleil = literary/poetic use only.

items.fullSentence: Il y a de l'orage prévu ce soir.
items.why: il y a de l'orage — orage (thunderstorm) is masculine and starts with a vowel, so de l' is used (elision of de la or de le before a vowel). du would be used if there were no vowel elision needed; here the vowel triggers de l' regardless of gender. des would be plural (des orages).

items.fullSentence: Il y a beaucoup de nuages aujourd'hui.
items.sentenceTrans: There are a lot of clouds today.
items.why: beaucoup de nuages — after a quantity expression (beaucoup, peu, trop, assez, plein), the partitive article is always replaced by plain de (no article). So NOT beaucoup des nuages. This is a general rule: beaucoup de + noun regardless of gender. Without a quantity word you would say il y a des nuages.

items.sentenceTrans: It has been raining since this morning.
items.why: il pleut — from the verb pleuvoir, which only exists as an impersonal form. Present: il pleut. No other person or number. Do not say il fait pleuvoir — that would mean 'he makes it rain'. il y a de la pluie is grammatically fine but more formal/written; il pleut is the standard spoken form. pluie alone is a noun, not a verb.

items.contextLabel: [Checking forecast] Looking out the window in January
items.sentenceTrans: It's snowing a lot this week.
items.why: il neige — neiger is impersonal like pleuvoir: only il neige exists in present tense. neigeait is imperfect (past continuous); il fait de la neige is NOT standard French — you cannot use faire + de la neige. il y a de la neige is correct but refers to snow already on the ground; il neige = it is snowing (actively falling).

items.contextLabel: [Checking forecast] Asking about the weather — complete the FORMAL question
items.fullSentence: Quel temps fait-il à Lyon en ce moment ?
items.sentenceTrans: What's the weather like in Lyon right now?
items.why: Quel temps fait-il ? — the standard question form. Quel is an interrogative adjective agreeing with temps (masculine singular). The inversion fait-il marks it as formal/standard. Il fait quel temps ? is also correct and common in casual spoken French (no inversion). Comment il fait mixes two different question structures incorrectly. Qu'est-ce que le temps is not a real French structure.

recap.note: general weather — never il est or c'est
frais = cool; doux = mild; lourd = muggy

recap.example: Il y a du vent / du soleil / du brouillard.

recap.form: il y a de l' + vowel noun
recap.note: elision before vowel regardless of gender

recap.example: Il y a beaucoup de nuages.

standard question; il fait quel temps ? = casual
